summary: This document fixes weaknesses in OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication when keys are managed manually. The existing mechanism is vulnerable to replay attacks within and across sessions, and this extension adds protections against them.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF can protect its packets with a cryptographic digest, but when the key is set up by hand there were two gaps. An attacker could record a packet and send it again later, and the address in the IP header was not covered by the digest at all. This RFC closes both gaps: the packet counter becomes 64 bits wide and survives a reboot, and the source address is folded into the calculation.

questions: how does ospf prevent replay attacks
what is the ospf boot count
why is the ip source address in the ospf hash
subtitle: Closing the replay and IP-header holes in OSPF's cryptographic authentication when keys are configured by hand.

tldr.problem: OSPF's cryptographic authentication with manual keys could be defeated by replaying packets from an earlier session, and the IP header was not covered by the digest at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the OSPF sequence number to 64 bits, with a boot count in the upper half, and puts those 8 octets after the packet where the digest covers them. It also folds the IP source address into the digest and gives OSPF its own cryptographic protocol ID.
tldr.outcome: The new mechanism is authentication type 3, and a router that does not implement it simply drops the packets, so an old and a new router can share a network without misreading each other.

facts.label: Authentication type
facts.value: 3, cryptographic authentication with extended sequence numbers

today: RFC 7474 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track. It updates RFC 2328 and RFC 5709, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes it. It covers only the case where OSPF keys are configured by hand, and says that automatic key management is out of scope.

sections.title: What Was Wrong With the Old Mechanism
sections.content:
The OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication mechanism as described in RFC 2328 uses per-packet sequence numbers to provide protection against replay attacks. The sequence numbers increase monotonically so that attempts to replay stale packets can be thwarted. The sequence number values are maintained as part of neighbour adjacency state, so if an adjacency is taken down the associated sequence numbers are reinitialised and neighbour adjacency formation starts over again. The mechanism also does not specify how to deal with the rollover of a sequence number when its value wraps. These omissions can be exploited by attackers to implement various replay attacks.

The cryptographic authentication as described in RFC 2328, and later updated in RFC 5709, does not include the IP header, and this omission can be exploited to launch several attacks, because the source address in the IP header is not protected. The OSPF specification requires implementations, for broadcast and NBMA networks, to use the source address in the IP header to determine the neighbour from which a packet was received. Changing the IP source address of a packet to a conflicting address can therefore be used to produce denial-of-service attacks.

If the packet is interpreted as coming from a different neighbour, the received sequence number state for that neighbour may be incorrectly updated, which may disrupt communication with a legitimate neighbour. Hello packets may be reflected to cause a neighbour to appear to have one-way communication, and Database Description packets may be reflected when the per-packet sequence numbers are sufficiently divergent, in order to disrupt an adjacency.

RFC 2328 states that implementations MUST offer keyed MD5 authentication, and the RFC notes it is likely that this will be deprecated in favour of the stronger algorithms described in RFC 5709 and required in RFC 6094. This document defines a few simple changes to the cryptographic authentication mechanism as currently described in RFC 5709, to prevent such IP-layer attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things went wrong. The counter that makes each packet unique was tied to the neighbour relationship, so a router that restarted or rebuilt a relationship began counting again and old packets looked fresh. And the address in the IP header was never covered by the digest, so an attacker could rewrite it and the receiver would think the packet came from a different neighbour.

sections.title: Replay Protection With a 64-bit Sequence Number
sections.content:
To provide replay protection against both inter-session and intra-session replay attacks, the OSPFv2 sequence number is expanded to 64 bits, with the least significant 32-bit value containing a strictly increasing sequence number and the most significant 32-bit value containing the boot count. OSPFv2 implementations are required to retain the boot count in non-volatile storage for the deployment life of the OSPF router. The requirement to preserve the boot count is also placed on SNMP agents by the SNMPv3 security architecture, through the snmpEngineBoots variable.

Since there is no room in the OSPFv2 packet for a 64-bit sequence number, it occupies the 8 octets following the OSPFv2 packet and MUST be included when calculating the OSPFv2 packet digest. These additional 8 octets are not included in the OSPFv2 packet header length, but they are included in the OSPFv2 header Authentication Data length and the IPv4 packet header length.

The lower-order 32-bit sequence number MUST be incremented for every OSPF packet sent by the OSPF router. On reception, the sequence number MUST be greater than the sequence number in the last OSPF packet of that type accepted from the sending OSPF neighbour; otherwise the packet is considered a replayed packet and dropped. OSPF packets of different types may arrive out of order if they are prioritised as recommended in RFC 4222.

OSPF routers implementing this specification MUST use available mechanisms to preserve the strictly increasing property for the deployed life of the router, including cold restarts. This is achieved by maintaining a boot count in non-volatile storage and incrementing it each time the router loses its prior sequence number state. The SNMPv3 snmpEngineBoots variable MAY be used for this purpose, but maintaining a separate boot count solely for OSPF sequence numbers decouples SNMP reinitialisation from OSPF reinitialisation. In the rare event that the lower-order 32-bit sequence number wraps, the boot count can be incremented to preserve the strictly increasing property of the aggregate sequence number, so a separate OSPF boot count is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The counter becomes twice as wide. The lower half counts packets as before, and the upper half counts how many times the router has lost its state, which it stores permanently. Together the two halves keep increasing for the life of the router, so a packet recorded before a restart can never look new.

sections.title: The OSPF Packet Changes
sections.content:
The OSPF packet header includes an authentication type field, and 64 bits of data for use by the appropriate authentication scheme, which is determined by the type field. Authentication types 0, 1 and 2 are defined in RFC 2328, and this section defines authentication type 3.

When this authentication scheme is used, the 64-bit Authentication field in the OSPF packet header is changed: the sequence number is removed, the Key ID is extended to 32 bits and moved to the former position of the sequence number, and the 0 field at the start of the OSPFv2 header authentication is extended from 16 bits to 24 bits. The 64-bit sequence number is moved to the first 64 bits following the OSPFv2 packet, where it is protected by the authentication digest. These additional 64 bits, or 8 octets, are included in the IP header length but not in the OSPF header packet length.
sections.plainLanguage: The header gains a wider key identifier, and the counter moves out of the header and into the space just after the packet, where the digest covers it. The header's length field is not changed, so the packet looks the same size to anything that only reads the header.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Key
sections.content:
This section describes how the security solution selects long-lived keys from key tables, selecting the key and the corresponding Security Association as defined in RFC 5709. Generally, a key used for OSPFv2 packet authentication should satisfy three requirements: for packet transmission, the key validity interval as defined by SendLifetimeStart and SendLifetimeEnd must include the current time; for packet reception, the interval defined by AcceptLifetimeStart and AcceptLifetimeEnd must include the current time; and the key must be valid for the desired security algorithm.

For unicast transmission, where a router R1 sends from its interface I1 to the interface I2 of a remote router R2, the key should be shared by both routers, so the Peers field must contain the area ID or, if no key containing the area ID is present, the string "all". The Direction field must be either "out" or "both", and the Interfaces field must match I1 or "all". If several keys match the interface, keys that explicitly match I1 are preferred over keys matching "all", and if there are still several, the key with the most recent SendLifetimeStart is selected, which facilitates graceful key rollover. The Key ID field in the OSPFv2 header is set to the selected key's LocalKeyName.

When R1 and R2 are connected by a virtual link, the Peers field must identify the virtual endpoint rather than the virtual link, and since there may be several virtual links to the same router, the transit area ID must be part of the identifier: the transit area ID, a colon, and the router ID. If no such key exists, a key with the Peers field set to the transit area ID is used, followed by a key with the Peers field set to "all". The Interfaces field is not used for key selection on virtual links.

For multicast transmission, to a multicast address such as AllSPFRouters or AllDRouters, the router first tries a key with the Peers field containing the area ID to which the interface belongs, and then a key with the Peers field "all". The Interfaces field must match the interface over which the packet is sent or "all", and the Direction field must be "out" or "both".

For reception, the ID of the authentication key is included in the authentication field of the OSPF packet header, and using this Key ID it is straightforward for a receiver to locate the corresponding key. The interface on which the key was received must be associated with the key's interface, the Key ID obtained from the packet header must correspond to the neighbour's PeerKeyName, and because OSPFv2 keys are symmetric the LocalKeyName and PeerKeyName are identical. The Direction field must be either "in" or "both", and the Peers field must match as described above.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key says which area it covers, which interfaces it is for, and which direction it may be used in. The router picks the most specific key that fits the packet it is sending, and the receiver picks the same key from the identifier carried in the header.

sections.title: Protecting the IP Header
sections.content:
This document updates the definition of the Apad constant, as defined in RFC 5709, to include the IP source address from the IP header of the OSPFv2 protocol packet. The overall cryptographic authentication process remains unchanged, and the First-Hash now includes the 64-bit sequence number along with the Authentication Trailer and the OSPF packet.

OSPF routers sending OSPF packets must initialise the first 4 octets of Apad to the value of the IP source address that would be used when sending the packet. The remainder of Apad contains the value 0x878FE1F3 repeated (L - 4)/4 times, where L is the length of the hash being used and is measured in octets rather than bits. On reception, implementations MUST initialise the first 4 octets of Apad to the IP source address from the IP header of the incoming packet, with the same remainder. The basic idea is to incorporate the IP source address in the cryptographic authentication computation, so that any change of IP source address in a replayed packet can be detected. This prevents all attacks where a rogue OSPF router changes the IP source address of a packet and replays it on the same multi-access interface or another interface, because the modification results in an authentication failure and the packet being dropped.

To prevent cross-protocol replay attacks for protocols sharing common keys, the two-octet OSPFv2 Cryptographic Protocol ID is appended to the authentication key prior to use. The result is a Protocol-Specific Authentication Key, Ks, which is always L octets long in this application. If Ks is exactly L octets long, then Ko is equal to Ks. If Ks is more than L octets long, Ko is set to H(Ks). If Ks is less than L octets long, Ko is Ks with zeros appended to the end so that Ko is L octets long. The rest of the mechanism described in RFC 5709 remains unchanged other than one detail that was unspecified: when XORing Ko and Ipad or Opad, Ko MUST be padded with zeros to the length of Ipad or Opad.
sections.plainLanguage: The digest now covers the address in the IP header, so a packet whose source address has been rewritten no longer matches. A two-byte protocol number is also added to the key before it is used, so a packet captured from one routing protocol cannot be replayed into another that happens to share the same key.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: This security extension uses a new authentication type, the AuType in the OSPFv2 header. When an OSPFv2 packet is received and the AuType does not match the configured authentication type for the interface, the packet is dropped as specified in RFC 2328. This guarantees backward-compatible behaviour consistent with any other authentication type mismatch.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that has not been upgraded will see an authentication type it does not recognise and drop the packet, exactly as it would for any other mismatch. Nothing has to be coordinated beyond the keys themselves.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document rectifies the manual key management procedure that currently exists within OSPFv2, as part of Phase 1 of the KARP Working Group, so only the OSPFv2 manual key management mechanism is considered. Any solution that takes advantage of automatic key management is beyond the scope of this document.

The sequence number extension offers most of the benefits of more complicated mechanisms without their attendant challenges, but there are a couple of drawbacks. First, it requires the OSPF implementation to be able to save its boot count in non-volatile storage. If that storage is ever repaired or upgraded such that the contents are lost, or the OSPFv2 router is replaced, the authentication keys MUST be changed to prevent replay attacks. Second, if a router is taken out of service completely, the potential exists for re-establishment of an OSPFv2 adjacency by replaying the entire session establishment. The RFC calls this scenario extremely unlikely, since it would imply an identical adjacency formation packet exchange, and notes that replaying Hello packets alone for a router that has been taken out of service should not result in any serious attack, as the only consequence is superfluous processing. That attack could also be thwarted by changing the relevant manual keys.

The document also provides a solution to prevent certain denial-of-service attacks that can be launched by changing the source address in the IP header of an OSPFv2 protocol packet. Using a single crypto sequence number can leave the router vulnerable to a replay attack where the same source IP address is used on two different point-to-point unnumbered links, so in such environments, where an attacker can actively tap the point-to-point links, it is recommended that different keys be used on each of those unnumbered IP interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The protection depends on the router remembering its boot count across restarts, so if that stored value is ever lost the keys have to be changed. And where the same source address is used on two different links, the RFC recommends a separate key for each.

fields.name: Packet length
fields.desc: Length of the OSPF packet in octets. It does not include the 8 octets of the sequence number extension.

fields.name: Router ID
fields.desc: The identifier of the sending router.

fields.name: Area ID
fields.desc: The area this packet belongs to.

fields.name: AuType
fields.desc: The authentication type. Type 3 is the one this RFC defines.

fields.name: Zero
fields.desc: Extended from 16 bits to 24 bits for this authentication type.

fields.name: Auth Data Len
fields.desc: Length of the authentication data, which now includes the 8 octets of the sequence number.

fields.name: Key ID
fields.desc: Extended to 32 bits and moved to the former position of the sequence number.

fields.name: Sequence Number (Boot Count)
fields.desc: The most significant 32 bits. Incremented whenever the router loses its sequence number state, and kept in non-volatile storage.

fields.name: Sequence Number (Strictly Increasing Packet Counter)
fields.desc: The least significant 32 bits. Incremented for every OSPF packet sent.

viz.caption: HOW A KEY IS CHOSEN FOR TRANSMISSION

items.title: Peers
items.text: The area ID of the link, or "all" if no key names the area.

items.title: Direction
items.text: "out" or "both" for sending, "in" or "both" for receiving.

items.title: Interfaces
items.text: The interface the packet leaves, or "all".

items.title: Most specific wins
items.text: A key naming the interface beats one saying "all".

items.title: Newest key wins
items.text: If several still match, the one with the most recent SendLifetimeStart, which makes key rollover smooth.

data.title: Apad
data.code:
First 4 octets:  the IP source address
Remaining octets: 0x878FE1F3 repeated (L - 4) / 4 times

L is the length of the hash, measured in octets.
